quote: And I do wanna understand that. Do you understand that address? If you don't mind giving it to me.
stewart_read: Rep is running the verify section as scripted, re-confirming the address methodically despite significant audio/transcription garble throughout the call.
coaching_implication: This is a fine baseline execution — no coaching action needed here, but it establishes the rep does understand the verify sequence.

quote: I just I was wondering how much it would cost and what's the rebates on it and all that, but I never got around to doing the rest of it.
stewart_read: The customer hands the rep a direct pricing/rebate question up front — exactly the scenario the price_estimate_before_design rebuttal is built for (redirect to design via a real number capture). The rep never uses this framing; instead she moves straight into address/title verification without acknowledging the cost curiosity at all.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic sequencing — rep may be deferring the cost answer until qualification is complete, which is standard setter practice.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to briefly acknowledge the cost question using the price_estimate_before_design framing ('totally fair to ask — cost depends on a few things, let me grab that info') so the customer feels heard before verification starts, rather than silently pivoting past it.

quote: Well, it says Amy is the homeowner. Are you on the title of the home as well?
stewart_read: The rep correctly identifies that the caller is not the homeowner and that the daughter (Amy) holds title, which is the right verify catch. However, the rep never circles back to ensure Amy will be present for the actual appointment/closer call.
alternative_hypothesis: The call never reaches booking stage, so this protocol step may be moot for this particular call.
coaching_implication: If a future appointment is set on this lead, the closer's brief must state that Amy (not this caller) is the title-holder and must be the one on the eventual proposal call.

quote: Well, yeah. So everything looks good here on my end.
stewart_read: Rep declares verification complete at this point without ever capturing a confident bill figure (the customer had just said 'I do not know' twice) and without having asked what interested the customer in solar. This is a premature completion call against the schema's 6-of-8 threshold expectation.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may consider the rough '$300 a month' estimate sufficient and is moving toward bill-document collection as the final remaining step, which is a legitimate sequencing choice.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to slow down before declaring verify 'done' — the interest-reason question was never asked at all on this call, a gap distinct from the bill-collection struggle that follows.

quote: K. Yeah. Probably $300 a month or so.
stewart_read: The customer eventually gives a rough dollar figure after several 'I don't know' responses, but the rep only echoes it back numerically and never flips it into emotional alignment-against-the-utility.
coaching_implication: This is the exact moment for the ask-acknowledge-flip pattern; the rep's next line should have reframed the $300/month as the reason to act, not just repeated the figure.

quote: Yeah. I don't see any I can here. They must do it online or something. Probably, the paperless is something.
stewart_read: The customer's paperless/online-bill disclosure is a clean trigger for the schema's alternative_paths (shifting to a website walkthrough or scheduling verbal read-back), but the rep does not name or execute any specific alternative path — she simply proposes sending a generic follow-up request.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be constrained by the fact that the caller is not the actual account holder and genuinely cannot access Amy's online utility account, making a live pivot impossible on this call regardless of protocol.
coaching_implication: Even if live capture isn't possible today, the rep should explicitly offer to text Amy directly for the online bill screenshot per the shopping_customer_protocol pattern, rather than leaving the follow-up vague and requestor-less.

quote: Hey. Awesome. Well, thank you for your time, and we will stay in touch.
stewart_read: The call ends with no date, no time, no appointment, and no explicit next-step ownership — a passive close rather than a locked callback or booked appointment.
coaching_implication: Replay this ending with the rep: contrast against the button_up template requiring a stated day/time and the 'is that fair?' handshake. Even a callback outcome needs a locked time, which never happened here.

quote: I just I I just I just I'm not too sure that we could see your very good design just because of how much trees you do have. Would you be Would you be Would you be, like, trimming trees or cutting any down?
stewart_read: The rep raises shading/trees as a possible design obstacle and asks about tree removal — the customer's answer that the backside and front get full sun before sunset is a positive signal the rep could anchor on, but she doesn't reflect it back as reassurance or momentum.
coaching_implication: When a customer describes strong sun exposure despite tree concerns, the rep should explicitly reflect that back ('that's great news for your design') to build momentum rather than moving straight to the next verify item.
